en: Salutations to the illustrious Hayagrīva.
From the drama *Jānakīpariṇaya*:
"As if closely joined."

First Act. I bow to the lotus-eyed Lord of Ramā, who reclines upon the king of serpents, whose evil eyes have been cast away, who has undertaken the protection of the entire world, who is the abode of a multitude of virtues, and who is praised by the gods; I worship Him who, following the intoxicating nectar of the Upaniṣadic teachings, seems to drink in the sandalwood dust from the slopes of the breasts of the beauties of Vraja.
I bow to the supreme deity, adorned with the Śrīvatsa, the Kaustubha, and Lakṣmī— the most excellent jasmine creeper in the forest of Vedānta.
I shall explain, according to my understanding, the seven-act drama titled *Śrījānakīpariṇaya*, composed by the sacrificer named Rāmabhadra.

In this regard, the celebrated poet known as Śrī Rāmabhadradākṣita has composed a work centered on the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*). It features the hero in the form of Rāma, who is *dhīrodātta* (calm and noble), and the antagonist in the form of Rāvaṇa, who is *dhīroddhata* (calm yet haughty). It consists of seven acts. [The *dhīrodātta* hero is defined as follows: "One who is exceedingly profound in great courage like Jānakī, patient, free from boastfulness, whose pride is concealed within, and firm in his vows, is called *dhīrodātta*."
Abounding in pride and envy, devoted to deceit and guile,
he is haughty, seductive, fickle, fierce, and boastful.

This latter ten-act drama, *Jānakīpariṇaya*, is a worthy successor to that [other] drama. May the lotus-foot of the Lord of the Universe protect you—the foot which is licked by the tongues of the cows approaching with great joy at the abundant sound of the blossoming flute, and which is the beloved of the young deer.

Commencing this drama entitled *Pariṇaya*, the author first composes at the outset the *nāndī*—consisting of twelve words, endowed with auspicious benedictions, and constituting the primary limb of the *pūrvaraṅga* which serves as an obstacle-remover—for the purpose of warding off impediments, beginning with the words "saṃsaktān."

[He] approaches those who are ever-attached to the lotus-thicket of the Vedānta through their constant sporting [in it], and who are eternally bound to His lotus-feet. "Upaniṣad" means that in which the highest good (*śreyas*) sits near; thus, "Vedānta" is the *upaniṣad*. These [Vedāntas] are the *aupaniṣadas*. Their very utterances—the sentences themselves—are like honey-sweet juices (*mādhvī-rasa*).
By this, the Lord's being knowable through the Vedānta and the fact that the *upaniṣads* constitute the essence as compared to the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) are manifested.

Here, there is the figure of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor); its definition, as stated in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, is: "The metaphor (*tadrūpaka*) is the non-difference between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*).
[The word] *pātum* means "as if to taste" or "to savor. Here, there is the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).
The definition of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is: "It is the imagining of something else [in place of] the subject at hand.

Thus, for the cowherd women (*gopikās*) who, having lifted up Kṛṣṇa—the ever-newly beautiful youth—place upon the surface of their chests the bliss of his embrace, there are the particles of sandalwood paste (*pāṭīra-reṇu*), that is, the dust of the sandalwood applied to the slopes of their breasts (*kucataṭī*). [These are the objects of the fancy.]

"As if to cleanse," that is, as if to purify. Here too there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). The cows—the female cattle—approaching the vicinity of Kṛṣṇa, drawn by the abundant and excessive joy (*āmoda*) produced by the sound of the flute (*muralī*), the divine wind-instrument being played; [the word] *upasīdadgavyaḥ* (or *upasīdadgavī*) is formed by adding the suffix *ṭac* according to the rule "gorataddhitaluki" and then the feminine suffix *ṅīp* by the rule "ṭiṅketiṅīp.
By their tongues—that is, their palates—it was licked, meaning tasted.

"An animal knows it, a child knows it, and a serpent knows the essence of song"—thus is established by scripture the cows' fondness for singing. [This concludes] the section on singing. [The plot is developed] through the acts of the Opening, the Progression, the Development, the Pause, and the Conclusion; the previous nature [of the characters] remains as in the case of other [characters], like those who hold the primary office.
That drama is declared to be one in which either the hero or the heroine is described as the primary figure, and which is endowed with a well-known protagonist.
The attainment of the fruit is declared to be like that of the seed and the drop.
Thus [it is said].
That which the actors perform before the commencement of the drama for the purpose of pacifying obstacles is designated as the *pūrvaraṅga*.
Although there are many constituent parts of the preliminary rite (*pūrvaraṅga*) in a drama,
nevertheless, the *nāndī* must necessarily be performed for the sake of pacifying obstacles.
Thus it has been fully proclaimed.
[Regarding] the gods, the twice-born, the king, and others... First Act.

Having wiped the dust from my feet, I applied red lac to them; having rubbed away the saffron-paste from her breasts, I fashioned leaf-designs with ashes.
May Dākṣāyaṇī protect you—she who, upon seeing her circle of female friends speaking words of "wander at your own will," merely bowed with a sidelong glance full of intentional meaning.
The sense is that licking the feet of cows is the natural disposition of calves.
"Alīka" means false; it refers to the cowherd boy Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

The underlying meaning is that since the Supreme Self is, in ultimate reality, devoid of birth and other such attributes, His assuming forms such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa is merely an illusion (māyāmātra); thus, His state as a cowherd boy is unreal.
*Pādāmbuja*: like a lotus, a lotus-foot;
*caraṇāravinda*. *Vaḥ*: you (plural).
May the protector preserve [us].
Regarding the Śārdūlavikrīḍita meter, its definition is: "Śārdūlavikrīḍita consists of [the sequence] ma, sa, ja, sa, ja, ta, ta, followed by a guru (long syllable).
This is its characteristic.

In this work, the protagonist is the Supreme Self (paramātman) taught in the Upaniṣads, who has assumed the form of Rāma as a mere sport; the antagonist, Rāvaṇa, will likewise assume a false form of Rāma through illusion along with Vidyutjihva—this is the meaning of the poem, which is rooted in the Upaniṣads and slightly indicated by the words *jihvā* and *ṛ*.
Considering that the removal of obstacles is even greater when the auspicious rite itself is more abundant, he states the second *nāndī* verse beginning with "śamyā kasya."

O Dākṣāyaṇī, at your feet— at your two feet (*caraṇe* being used in the singular by way of genus)— when Śiva performed a deep prostration at the pair of your feet to appease you after you had cast him out in anger, [the pollen] of the *śamyāka* flower, the *āragvadha*, which was clinging to the edge of his crown,
was wiped away; it was cleansed by me—
by me, your friend.
There, barley-gruel mixed with lac-dye was applied and smeared.

upon your two breasts, which are as tender as buds.
Ash— that which was spoken [as being] connected to the body of Śiva by one whose limbs are pitiless—

therein, a leaf-sprout is the growth of leaves in the form of *makarika* and the like.
Created; fashioned;
therefore.
"Svacchandam" means according to one's desire; since the shame of this [worldly] enjoyment has been cast off, it means "shamelessly. "Vihara" means move about in the presence of the guru and others.
Or rather: "Play with your husband as you please today, in such a way that the application of red lac, the decorative leaf-designs, and so forth may be completely wiped away.
Thus, with intent—that is, with a meaningful purpose according to the aforementioned manner—she speaks with significance.
One by whom speech—that is, words—has been uttered or spoken;
[addressing] the circle of friends, that is, the group of female companions;
with a crooked or artful manner.
By sight alone— that is, by vision itself— and not by the mind;
indeed!
Is it not correct?

[The form] *natī* means "striking. [One might argue: "Is *ānati* not a single word? If that were the case, then by the rule *āṅo rāmahanaḥ*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) suffix would apply, and the form would have to be *ānāneti*.
Dākṣāyaṇī, the daughter of Dakṣa, namely Śivā,
may she protect you all.
[End of the *Jānakīpariṇaya* at the conclusion of the play.]
Sūtradhāra:

(Looking ahead) This man is an expounder of the scriptures, proficient in the established doctrines of Bharata’s system; he is the pinnacle of excellence for those who compose poetry in its refined form.
He promotes the welfare of the virtuous gathered in this assembly, which is accessible only through merit, and he is worthy of veneration by all.
"May he protect you!

Having seen the mark of Śivā’s play—dust from the bed-chamber marked by the pollen of her anklets—as she returned from the bridal chamber, Śiva prostrated himself at night and embraced her firmly. Because the subtle meaning is revealed through the words of the clever friend, this is the *sūkṣma* (subtle) ornament.
Its definition is: "The *sūkṣma* [ornament] is said to be the revelation of a subtle meaning that was previously unperceived."

Here, by the word "kuṭilayā" (by the crooked one), the crooked path of the poet's meaning—consisting of the assumption of false forms such as Rāma and so forth, residing in Rāvaṇa and others—is indicated.
The meter is as before.
"Not blind darkness."

The verse prescribed at the beginning of dramatic compositions such as the *nāṭaka* is the *nāndī*. At its end—that is, at its conclusion—once the *sūtradhāra* has entered for the *pūrvaraṅga* and departed after reciting the *nāndī*, which constitutes the principal part of the *pūrvaraṅga*, another *sūtradhāra* enters and speaks; this is the implied meaning.

For it has been stated: "Having first performed the *pūrvaraṅga* and the *sūtradhāra* having exited, another actor enters and causes the drama (*kāvyam*) to be narrated. As for the definition of the *sūtradhāra*: "One who brings forth the merits of the author, the plot, and the subject matter..."
The stage-manager, skilled in the decoration of the stage, says: "Ho! Let it be so!"
He speaks.
Of the *śāstras*, that is, of all the branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) beginning with the *Ṛgveda*. He is their "proclaimer" (*pravaktā*), meaning one who has correctly mastered them.

In the expression "of the *śāstras*," the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), according to the rule "the sixth case is used for the agent or the object when a word ending in the suffix *kṛt* follows."
The "opinion" (mata) refers to the intention of the sage Bharata, the originator of drama; it means the treatise composed by him. Its "established conclusion" (siddhānta) is its definitive doctrine.
Skilled and capable in the *tantra*,
[he attends to] those poets who have come together to obtain titles and the like that proclaim their own excellence.
Among those composing poetry...
The excellence— the state of being most preeminent— of charming poetry, that is, of poetic composition filled with the sentiments (*rasa*) such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*),
and the attainment of titles and honors indicative of such high distinction,
is easily obtainable through a single act of merit alone.
This assembly, this congregation of virtuous and noble beings.

that which is more excellent;

Or rather, [it refers to] the excellence of fresh poetry—that is, the locus of pre-eminence;
the meaning is: one who possesses the highest degree of fresh poetry.
The assembly of the virtuous is the first act.

Therefore, by now presenting to this man—who is preeminent in praiseworthy qualities—the science of dramatic representation inherited through my lineage, according to the doctrine of Bharata-ācārya, I shall make myself successful.

Of those who have come from various places;

the remainder is as before.

The meter is *śikhariṇī*, according to its definition: "The *śikhariṇī* consists of the syllables *ya*, *ma*, *na*, *sa*, *bha*, *la*, *ga*, divided by the [six] rasas and the [three] svas. Here, because the epithets such as "proclaimer of the scriptures" and so forth contain an implied intention regarding the capacity for being worshipped by all, there is the poetic figure *parikara*.
The definition of *parikara* as an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is: "It occurs when a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) is intended with a specific purpose."

I shall make myself, me, one who has accomplished his purpose—that is, I shall make him fulfilled and one whose aim is realized.

As for the term *sāmājikāḥ*: they are those who assemble (*samavayanti*) in a social gathering (*samāja*, i.e., an assembly), namely, the members of the audience (*sabhyāḥ*).

that [work] is "newly composed," meaning fashioned with novelty.

That by which something is represented (*rūpyate*) is a *rūpaka*; a drama (*nāṭaka*), which is primarily characterized by dramatic representation (*abhinaya*), is what is denoted by the term *rūpaka*.

Rāma: You have spoken rightly, lady.
There dwells upon the trunk of a *nīpa* tree a peacock with shimmering tail-feathers, and here wanders a deer with long outer corners of its eyes, grazing on the grassy sward.
This elephant touches the sallakī tree on its high branch with his trunk; O lotus-eyed one, to whom would this forest region not be pleasing?

Moreover: Does the peacock not bear the beauty of your mass of hair upon its crest? Does the deer not partake in the loveliness of your eyes in its gaze? O Noble Lord, that very forest—filled with flocks of variegated beasts and birds—delights my heart through the sounds of their cries; for by mentioning a part, the whole is understood. They are driven away, that is, removed to a distance.
Does the bed fashioned from tender sprouts not surpass, indeed exceed, the bed of swan-down—the couch made of swan’s down?
This is the meaning of "surpasses.
By means of a livelihood consisting of wild fruits—sweet and delightful due to their unique ripening—the urban way of life is caused to be forgotten, brought to oblivion.
8. Regarding "nīpa": [it refers to] the *nīpa* tree.

The peacock, whose tail-feathers—the mass of plumage—are shining brilliantly, dwells upon the trunk of a *nīpa* tree (the term *skandha* refers to the trunk; see Amarakośa: "The word *skandha* is not feminine and denotes the trunk").
This deer, with its long outer corners of the eyes, grazes—meaning it eats—the *śāda*, or young grass, in this *śādvala*, a place abounding in fresh grass.
This elephant, that great tusker, touches with his frontal globe—that is, the region of his forehead—the *sallakī* tree (known as the "elephant's favorite") upon its branch or bough;
therefore, O lotus-eyed one, O Padmākṣī, to whom would this forest region not be pleasing? [The meter is Mandākrāntā.]
"He holds," so it is said.

The peacock bears the beauty of a mass of *ghamilla* hair upon its crest, and the intoxicated elephant bears the splendor of your breasts upon its head; therefore, O young woman, I think that this forest beauty displays its likeness to you. (13)
Sītā—(With affection;
to herself) My noble husband has begun to praise me.
Therefore, I shall turn his heart elsewhere.

(Aloud: My noble lord, who are these deer playing? They have mouths with lower fangs as tender and white as a cluster of fresh lotus stalks, and their bodies possess a luster like the light of the full moon.

And who are these other deer wandering about? Their long, flowing manes are as white as the mass of foam produced by the collision of the series of waves from the milk-ocean of the moon’s rising; their eyes are tremulous and their pupils darting. Rāma: Ah, daughter of Janaka, these are lion cubs at play.
And these camari deer, startled by the sight of him, are fleeing;
behold them now!
1. Noble son, you have begun to describe me.
Therefore, I shall draw his heart away from elsewhere.

Noble son, who are these deer that frolic here, their broad mouths formidable with the buds of fangs as pure and tender as a cluster of fresh lotus stalks, and their bodies white as the moonlight of the full moon?

And who are these other deer that wander about, their long, swaying tails white as masses of foam produced by the mutual clashing of the waves of the milk-ocean at the moment of the moon’s rising, and their eyes with pupils darting to and fro?
Does the deer not possess the splendor of your eyes?
Does the spotted antelope not partake in the fortune and beauty of your gaze?
And does the rutting elephant not bear the glory of your breasts upon the position of its head, namely, its frontal globes?
Therefore, O young woman, O Sītā, I believe that this beauty of the forest reveals its similarity with you. This is the figure of speech *pratīpa* (the inverse). [In the Śārdūlavikrīḍita meter...]
From one place to another;
I cast forth, I impel;
it returns.
They possess mouths that are formidable, jagged, and wide, like clusters of fresh lotus stalks—streaks that are stainless, clear, tender, and beautiful;
their bodies are of a hue identical to the moonlight of the full moon;
they sport and play.

This forest brings joy to the eyes: its multitude of waves in the milk-ocean, churned and turbid at the moment of the moon’s rising, produces foam through their mutual friction; it contains herds of young yaks terrified by the playful lion-cubs, tigers emerging from caves that drag away leopards, and fierce ruru deer crying out; and it presents a scene where monkeys, agitated and shrieking as they are stung by bees driven from their nests in mid-flight, scatter in every direction. Fifth Act. The herd of young yaks, frightened by the playful lion-cubs; the tiger drawn from its cave by the leopard; the fierce ruru deer crying out; and the swarm of monkeys shrieking in distress as they are stung by bees shaken from their nests in the midst of their flight—this forest provides such a spectacle for the eyes.
Sītā—(Seeing them) Truly, there are honeycombs as large as great heaps of grain, hanging from the thickets of *tinisa* trees;
yet they are not easily obtainable by monkeys who have been driven away by the bees.
Rāma—Indeed so.
Sītā: Such is the conduct of those who have half of another's wealth!
Just as one person enjoys the interest deposited by another, so too this clever man, having remembered honey, has taken and is tasting it from the honeycomb with his finger.
1. On the branches of the *tiniśa* trees, there hang honeycombs the size of a *droṇa*, filled with swarms of great bees;
yet they are not easily obtained by monkeys who are harassed by those very bees. 2. Such is the nature of a person devoted solely to wealth.
Just as one person experiences an object deposited by another—
just as a skillful man, having taken the honey collected by that swarm of honey-bees, tastes it—
those whose hair or locks are like white, flickering, and long heaps of grain.
Those whose eyes have pupils (tāraka) and irises (kanīnika) that are extremely tremulous (taralatarā) and utterly deceptive (atyantavañcala); "the Śābas" refers to Śiva; "startled" means terrified;
"camarīs" refers to a specific species of deer.
"Playing," it says.
It was a place where herds of *camarī* yaks were terrified by playful, frolicking lion cubs;
where buffaloes were dragged away by tigers emerging from mountain caves;
and where there was a fierce, intense method of combat between various species of *ruru* deer and wild boars.

This forest brings about a fruit for the eyes—that is, it provides a purpose for them—wherein a troop of monkeys (*kīśakula*) stands, their faces bitten by honey-bees (*saraghā*) that have been shaken off, cast away, or driven off during the state of the extraction, drawing out, or removal of honey-wine (*mādhvīka*); consequently, the monkeys are distressed and utter a confused, clamorous sound. (Śārdūlavikrīḍita meter)
On the branches of the *tiniśa* trees—that is, on the branches of the *khadira* trees—there are honeycombs containing a *droṇa* measure of honey and eight *āḍhakas* of *adhvīkā* wine.
"Honeycombs" (*kṣaudrapaṭala*) refers to the honey (*madhu*) produced by small bees (*kṣudrābhir makṣikābhiḥ*). These are the three types of honey.

WHEA194 In the *Jānakīpariṇaya*, Rāma:—(To himself) This estimation of her toward me is that she does not regard me as being motivated by worldly gain. (Aloud) One person experiences what has been bestowed by another through the power of destiny.
Behold: the Mind-born [God of Love] places honey, whose sweetness is mockingly surpassed, upon your lower lip.
O Daughter of the King of Mithilā, why does this person not drink it after taking hold of it?
Sītā—(To herself: My noble husband’s longing has surpassed even my own prayers. (She stands with her face cast down in bashfulness. Rāma—(To himself: Now she feels ashamed at these words of mine;
for:
With the circles of my cheeks bristling with horripilation and the corners of my eyes betraying my burgeoning love,
neither my lotus-face nor even my mind bows down out of fear of others.
I shall show you another.
(Aloud: Look, Jānakī!
Though this Bakula tree is not even worthy of being sprinkled by the honey from your mouthfuls, it itself manifests such auspicious blossoms so that they may be worn by you every day.
1. It surpasses the expectation of the noble son.
These accumulations are solidified portions (from which honey is pressed); for one intent on wealth, that is, one attached to wealth;
"deposited" means placed or gathered.
It departs.

O Sītā, daughter of the King of Mithilā, this Love (Manobhava), who is yours, places honey—surpassing the essence of nectar and mocking the luster of the moon—upon this lower lip of yours; does this person, Rāma, not drink that honey of the lip, having somehow with great difficulty secured it?
(The meter is Puṣpitāgrā.)
"Conversing" means talking together.
"Ud" [is a prefix].
"With bristling hair" means with the hair on the body standing erect (*udgataromāñcam*).
"That which has the orb of the cheeks" refers to that whose region of the temples (*kapoladeśa*) is thus characterized.

"That in which the corners of the eyes are indicative of love"—love being expanded, increased, and intense affection (*praṇaya*), its "indicator" (*piśuna*) is the outer corner of the eye (*apāṅga*), and that [face] is so described because it possesses such corners.
She does not merely bow her own lotus-face toward the lotus-face of another;
rather, she inclines even my mind, making it devoted to him.
"From you," [it says].

O beloved, by the scent of your mouth-wine (*gaṇḍūṣamadhunaḥ*) wafting through the cardinal and intermediate directions, the *vakula* trees— acting as bees (*pañcama*) with their honeyed breath— have formed rows of blossoms that mock the braid of your hair, O dear one.
Sītā—(To herself) As my noble husband attended upon me in dreams with flattering words during those moments of longing, so now he attends upon me in person; it is wonderful, truly wonderful!

(Aloud) My noble husband, do you not see how this *adaśī* tree, adorned with clusters of blossoms that have burst forth at the end of the summer day, possessing the tender hue of a fresh *cūta* mango, graces this spot?
Rāma—(To himself: We have been skillfully mocked by her exchange of words and replies.
(Aloud: O Jānakī, you who are curious to see the forest!
Just as in dreams and in states of imagination, my son used to attend to me with affectionate words and other such gestures.

"It is truly marvelous, truly marvelous, how this is now manifesting before our very eyes! Noble son, do you not see? This *atasī* tree, adorned with clusters of blossoms that shine incessantly and possess a tender, dark hue like a fresh cloud expanding at the close of a summer day, graces this region."

Even though this *kesara* (or *vakula*) tree is devoid of—that is, lacking—the sprinkling or enjoyment of wine poured from the mouth, which constitutes the longing previously described, it nevertheless manifests in this way, displaying its own flowers that are worthy of you, appropriate, auspicious, and beautiful.

In the cardinal directions such as the east and the intermediate directions such as the southeast, the bees—drawn by the fragrance and scent of those flowers spreading and pervading—are stationed in rows and gathered in swarms; O beloved, they imitate and emulate your braid-like creeper, that tress resembling a creeping vine.
This is the figure of speech *upamā* (simile). [Śārdūlavikrīḍita meter].
In the states of imagination— conditions of mental activity directed toward the prospect of union with the beloved—
[they appear] through endearing words and playful speech;
they possess a dark, tender, and beautiful luster, like a fresh cloud expanding and growing at the close of a summer day during the rainy season.
With dense clusters of blossoms that have opened wide in continuous, gentle smiles (suggesting horripilation), the *atasī* tree—the dark ascetic tree (suggesting Rāma)—is skillfully [described].
"Skillfully" means...

In this *Jānakīpariṇaya*, let there be heard everywhere the dialogue and counter-dialogue, as well as the elements bearing blue, white, reddish-brown, and green hues, where mountain rivers flow with charming lotuses;
for in that place, O fierce lady, the tinkling of your jeweled girdle is indeed slightly followed by the cries of the swans who have become rustic from their playful quarrels.
Sītā—(To herself;

looking about) Since my noble husband has now rejected my very life—which was previously sought after by him when he first asked for me—I, being angry, began to hasten toward the inner apartments to go there, having stepped upon the ground with my feet.
My noble husband reminds me of that.
Ah! I shall speak thus.
(Aloud) My lord, for me who has taken refuge at your mighty arms, what marvelous thing in this forest is there that cannot be seen?
By him, safety has been granted to the Rākṣasas dwelling in Janasthāna from the presence of [the enemy].

Furthermore, when my noble husband first set out, although he entreated me again and again to accompany him, I forbade his following me. Being thus provoked, I rebuked him with a knitting of my brows; then, as he began to hurry toward the inner apartments with his girdle jingling in his agitation, my noble husband reminded me of that.
Very well; I shall speak thus:
"O Lord, by me who have taken refuge in the staff-like arms of Your Majesty, what wonder in this forest cannot be asked about without fear?"
By him, fearlessness was granted to the sages dwelling in Janasthāna from the presence of the Rākṣasas.
By that action— consisting of speech in the form of statements, replies, utterances, and counter-utterances—
they were mocked, that is, imitated.
"Blue," it says.

Here, the mountain rivers— possessing clear and pure water, with beautiful lotuses blooming everywhere, and flowing on all sides from every direction (the accusative case is used here according to the rule *ubhasarvatasoḥ*);
bearing minerals that possess the luster of blue, white, tawny, red, green, black, yellow, crimson, and the color of palāśa leaves (referring to gold, silver, copper, orpiment, realgar, red ochre,
antimony, green vitriol, lead, iron, and cinnabar).
It has been said: "Gandhaka, bhrakamiyā, and other minerals are produced from mountains.
Let them be seen!

In which mountain river, due to the cries—the sounds—of a flock of swans who, out of playful quarrel—that is, a sportful dispute—are wandering excessively, performing much roaming; [let those minerals be seen].
Indeed, O fierce one (or at any time), O angry one, even the tinkling sound of your jeweled girdle is heard slightly as it follows after you. (Śārdūlavikrīḍita meter)
Having reproached or censured [her] with embarrassment, wonder, or shame;
an action in which the girdle or waistband is jingling—due to agitation, confusion, or anger. Act Five.
Rāma—(having heard).
(With his gaze fixed in the distance: Who is this Rākṣasa entering the depths of the Kovidāra forest, wearing a tiger skin and carrying an elephant's head impaled upon a trident?
"Lakṣmaṇa does not know this.
(Then Lakṣmaṇa enters. Lakṣmaṇa: Who is this Rākṣasa entering the Kovidāra grove? Very well.
"I shall seize him!
(He mimes taking up his weapon. Sītā—(Looking elsewhere) My noble lord, this is certainly not a grove of *kovidāra* trees, but rather a forest of *karṇikāra* trees;
this is certainly no demon.
Look, look!

Some hideous ogress is entering, bearing a belly that is swollen, difficult to carry, and deviating from its natural path— even more so than the weight of a cluster of *tuñcī* fruits with their mouths gaping wide with fangs.
Rāma: What do you see?
It was indeed said by me here.
Sītā: (Looking) You have surely entered that very place.
"It is certainly not a *rākṣasa*!
Śama—(to himself! How is it that she mocks me by designating me a *rākṣasa*?
(Looking.)
(Aloud: Wonderful, wonderful! Upon further inspection, the Rākṣasa has turned into my own form.
1. Noble son, this is certainly not a forest of Kovidāra trees, but rather a grove of Karṇikāras; this is certainly not a Rākṣasa. Look, look!

A certain Rākṣasī of hideous appearance enters, her mouth terrifying with fangs, her belly swollen and difficult to support even from the weight of her breasts which rise high like gourd-pumpkins, and her mind distracted by the burden of her protruding womb.
"Are you not entering yourself? Surely this is no Rākṣasa."
He acts like a tiger.

Wearing a tiger skin, armed with a trident, pierced and sewn into that trident, and possessing the head of an elephant—he who is this Rākṣasa entering the heart of the copper-flowered forest of Kovidāra trees? Who is he?

*Karṇikāra* refers to the *āragvadha* tree. She is one whose face is *karāla*, meaning terrifying with fangs—that is, with protruding teeth. Like a *tumbī* fruit, that is, like a gourd fruit, [her belly] was heavy and large.
That whose navel is elevated and protruding;
a belly (*jaṭhara*) or abdomen that is difficult to bear, impossible to carry;
she whose form is difficult to behold, being hard to look upon—thus [describes] Sītā in the *Jānakīpariṇaya* (upon seeing him).
(With astonishment: Such a rakshasi bears my form! It has been seen by my noble lord. Rāma:—(Having looked:)
[With astonishment] What is the purpose of these two assuming such forms?
Sītā: Look, they have descended from the mountain peak.
Rāma: Do not say so!

For a person standing here, even objects at a distance of one *yojana* become visible to the eye. 198. Having entered the Kāñcanāravana grove, Lakṣmaṇa—(looking again with astonishment)—"Alas, alas! Even though I am armed and desirous of seizing him, my arrival here has become fruitless, since this Rākṣasa has hidden himself somewhere."
Furthermore,
it appears that the very purpose for which the slaughter of the Rākṣasa was promised has now occupied him for his own destruction as well.
For instance:
Carrying in his right hand a bow adorned with a golden band, and in the other a shaft fletched with heron feathers and tipped with a cluster of golden shafts,
he moves about casting his eyes here and there, as if searching for a night-stalker who has hidden his body somewhere.
2. 1. This rākṣasī too, having entered the karṇikāra grove, assumes my form;
let it be seen by the noble son.
2. Let us descend from the mountain peak and look.
Pointing out and defining;
having descended and settled;
the collection of things, the aggregate of objects, within the measure of a *yojana*, in places of one *yojana* extent.
"Cākṣuṣa" means that which is perceived by the eye;
"nilīnaḥ" means hidden or concealed;
"pratiśrutaḥ" means promised or pledged.
It has ceased and it has proceeded.

In his left hand, he carries a bow adorned with a golden band and fashioned with gold plates; in his other, right hand, he holds an arrow equipped with a golden shaft and joined with the wing-feathers of a *kaṅka* bird—a species of iron-backed fowl. Casting his eyes here and there, this Rāma moves forward as if searching for a night-stalker, a *rākṣasa*, whose body is concealed and hidden somewhere.
The poetic figure is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).
The meter is *pṛthvī*.
The Fifth Act.
199 (Reflecting:
But where, then, is the noble Jānakī?
Indeed, the upper plateau of the mountain has been ascended by these two noble ladies; how is it that only one noble man has descended?
(Looking upward.)
(With astonishment:
This noble one dwells upon the plateau of the mountain beneath a *vakula* tree, his splendor obscured by the clouds of fresh rain;
how is it that this noble man is here together with the noble daughter of the Earth, whose radiance has not yet fully returned?
Therefore, this must be that deceitful night-stalker who has assumed the form of a nobleman.
Hidden by a forest path dense with winding creepers, I shall follow him and watch. (He walks about.)
(Then enters Virādha, wearing the disguise of Rāma.
Virādha – (Seeing her) How is it that Jānakī is approaching from the Karṇikāra grove toward the Campaka bower?
(He approaches and observes her.)
Then enters Śūrpaṇakhā, assuming the form of Sītā.
Śūrpaṇakhā: I shall gather campaka flowers right here in this forest; Rāma’s brother-in-law will also come here.
Virādha: (Seeing her. To himself.)
This is Jānakī, possessed of unsurpassed beauty and grace.
(With wonder: Truly, this is an unprecedented creation of the Creator!
Or rather:
"I shall eat the campaka flowers right here in this forest;
the prince of the Raghu lineage will also come here."
Having studied.

"Aikṣvāka" means a male descendant of the lineage of Ikṣvāku;
[the word] "trātā" means a protector.
Saved means protected;
[he saved] the thorn of the three worlds, the enemy of the world.
Act Five.
Bharata: Venerable son of Kuśika, you must have this noble one consecrated here in the kingdom itself, and then he should be escorted into Ayodhyā.
Janaka: Oh, how impatient Bharata is for the delay!
Hanumān: These dear friends of my lord, Sugrīva, Vibhīṣaṇa, and the others, are likewise filled with longing.
Therefore, I shall cross the waters of the ocean accompanied by three monkeys.
(He exits.)
Janaka: My dear Śatrughna, summon the sages headed by Vasiṣṭha, as well as the family priests and ministers.
Śatrughna: As you command.
(He exits. Sītā: (To herself) My heart rejoices at the royal consecration of my noble husband, the conqueror of the gods of Laṅkā.

(Offstage) Let the beautiful, auspicious sandalwood paste, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice be prepared upon the excellent altar; let the jars filled with pure water, the parasol, and the fly-whisks be set in place.
My heart rejoices at the thought that the noble son, the victorious Lord of Laṅkā, is to be consecrated to the kingship.
"Utkaṇṭhante" means they long for or desire.
"Upasthāpaya" means bring near, cause to arrive, or—in other words—bring [it] here.
"Sajyantām" means let them be prepared.

On the auspicious altar for the coronation ceremony (paṭṭābhiṣeka-maṅgala-vedikā), let beautiful and delightful fragrant substances such as sandalwood and other perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice smeared with saffron be prepared and made ready. Let auspicious jars filled with water, the royal umbrella, and chowries be placed there.
Furthermore, let there be certain maidens present at that place.
Let the elephant, together with the horse, stay nearby or close at hand;
let the drums and kettledrums be beaten, for now—at this very moment—is the coronation of the Lord of the Raghus; therefore, let [all] be prepared—this is to be connected with what precedes.
Śārdūla...
60. In the *Jānakīpariṇaya*, some maidens are there; let them stay nearby, for the elephant and horse have grown weary, since the coronation of the Lord of the Raghus is imminent.
Janaka: This is the instruction of Vasiṣṭha. (Entering) Śatrughna: (To Rāma)
All have assembled.
(Then Vasiṣṭha enters.
Vasiṣṭha: Friend Kauśika, having seated Sītā and Rāma upon this throne, let us consecrate them together with the great ṛṣis and others.

Kauśika: As it pleases Maitrāvaruṇi. Janaka: Rāmabhadra has indeed honored the citizens and the people of the countryside with gifts of affection such as linen garments, ornaments, and other gifts. How is it that there is the sound of celestial drums in the sky, a rain of flowers, and the dancing of the Apsarases?
Kauśika: My child, what further favor may I bestow upon you?
Rāma: By your grace, my marriage to Jānakī has been accomplished without obstacle; having defeated the descendant of Pulastya along with his hosts in battle, this beloved wife has been recovered.

I have beheld Bharata, long desired, and even my consecration to the kingdom has been obtained. What else remains in this world that ought to be accomplished by you? [To Vasiṣṭha, the son of Mitrāvaruṇa: [He bows.]
*Kṣauma* refers to *dukūla* (fine silk).
*Naṭanārabhaṭī* means one whose garment is the stage for dancing. *Vivighnam* means "without obstacles."
In the battle, he has returned; after a long time, this Bharata, who was long desired, has been seen by all. After a long time, my long-desired consecration to the kingdom has also been obtained.
In this world, what other thing more dear than that remains to be accomplished by you? [Śārdūlavikrīḍita]...
Act Seven.
Nevertheless, let this be:
(The Benediction).
May men follow the path shown by Manu and others for the sake of their ultimate welfare; may kings, refraining from listening to the words of slanderers, protect the earth;
may poets be cherished with eloquent speech by people who possess a taste for aesthetic flavor; and may this poet’s devotion remain unshakable toward the Lord of the Raghus.
(Thus all exit.
Thus ends the seventh act in the play *Jānakīpariṇaya* composed by Śrī Rāmabhadra Dīkṣita.)
Oṃ tat sat.
This refers to what is about to be said.
The *bharatavākya* is the speech of the director of the performance.
Regarding the word "path" (*mārgam*):
Let human beings take recourse to the path shown by Manu and others for their own welfare—that is, for the sake of happiness in this world and the next.

Let kings also, being unswayed by the words of backbiters and informants—those who speak such things—and being thus blessed and virtuous, protect the earth. And let poets, whose expressions are full of aesthetic flavor (sarasokti), be constantly cherished and delighted by those who possess a refined taste for rasa.
Furthermore, may there be unwavering—that is, steadfast—devotion to the Lord Śrī Rāma, the sovereign of the Raghus, by this poet named Rāmabhadradīkṣita.
[This is composed in] the Śārdūlavikrīḍita meter.
I worship Mukunda, the root of bliss, whose beautiful lotus feet are worshipped by hosts of gods, who is free from duality,
and who gladdened Mucukunda.
Thus ends the commentary on the seventh act of the *Jānakīpariṇaya*, titled *Bālarañjanī*, a work by Śrī Śvetāraṇyanārāyaṇa Śarman.

May this [work] endure as long as the moon and sun, bringing auspiciousness to cows and Brahmins; may this land remain blessed with kings who serve the Vedas and the great scriptures. May we poets be cherished forever by those who know the essence of poetry, and may our devotion to the Lord of the Raghus, the God, remain unshakable.
